Nicolas Cage is making it clear — he’s not an “AI-friendly actor.”

The 62-year-old actor spoke out against a tech giant during an appearance at New York Comic Con on Saturday. He alleged that he was asked to sign an artificial intelligence waiver for the television series “Spider Noir.”

“Amazon is a very AI-friendly company, to the tune of $50 billion invested in OpenAI,” Cage said on stage.

“I am not an AI-friendly actor, so it’s like, connect those dots! I’m not a member of their club. I didn’t sign the waiver to let him use AI on ‘Spider-Noir.’ I’m probably not going to be working with that studio again, but that’s OK.”

Amazon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The use of AI continues to be a major sticking point across Hollywood. Industry unions including SAG-AFTRA and the Writers Guild recently secured protections against technology in new contracts. But as AI evolves and AI actors like Tilly Norwood continue to make headlines, it’s still unclear exactly how the industry will be affected.

“Spider-Noir,” which premiered in May, is a “Spider-Man” project that put a 1930s crime-thriller spin on the web-slinging superhero. The show was produced by both Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios.

Cage’s part as “The Spider” marked his first leading role in a series. The Oscar-winning actor, whose home in Malibu was recently affected by a sinkhole, is known best for his roles in movies like “National Treasure,” “Moonstruck” and “The Rock.”

Upon its release, “Spider-Noir” received much praise from fans and critics alike. In its first six weeks of streaming, the series earned 2.6 billion minutes watched, according to Nielsen. It was also Amazon’s most-nominated show at this year’s Emmys, with 11 nominations and five wins.

Last month, Amazon announced that the show was canceled after only one season, leaving much of the industry in shock.

During his Comic Con panel, Cage also said he plans to keep working in TV. He announced that he will be joining the HBO series “True Detective.”

“My agent’s out there somewhere listening,” Cage said. “That’s OK that I’m the first to announce that, right?”

title: I made the first I2PD client for iOS that works without Jailbreak
description: Experimental i2pd iPhone client. Contribute to SoItsTime/I2PdiOS development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
Source for an experimental iPhone app embedding i2pd. It includes an I2P browser, the local i2pd web console, router diagnostics, a searchable address book, and a shutdown Live Activity. It targets iOS 17 or later.

The repository contains source, the icon's SVG source, bootstrap names, and the i2pd patch. Vendor/, downloaded certificates, compiled libraries, the generated icon PNG, Xcode output, profiles, and local router data are ignored by Git. The bootstrap script retrieves i2pd's public reseed certificates into the ignored Vendor/ directory because verified reseeding requires them. No personal keys or certificates are supplied.

The app stores its router keys and address book in its own Application Support directory on the device. Those files are created at runtime and are never part of this repository.

The optional background audio loop is experimental. A background task offers limited extra time; iOS can still suspend or terminate the app. The router should not be relied on for continuous background service. Thanks to XITRIX, the developer of iTorrent, for the background audio approach that inspired this implementation.

The built-in browser accepts only .i2p destinations and uses i2pd's loopback SOCKS proxy. JavaScript starts disabled. The router's HTTP and SOCKS proxies bind to loopback. This is a prototype, and a successful build does not establish that connectivity or background execution will work on every device.

title: Microsoft 365 subscribers set to lose up to 4 TB of OneDrive storage
description: What Microsoft giveth, Microsoft taketh away, again and again
fullText:
What Microsoft giveth, Microsoft taketh away, again and again

Microsoft 365 subscribers on Family, Premium, or Pro tiers who make full use of their OneDrive storage allotments consider this a warning: It's fixin' to shrink.

Redmond published a support page this week detailing changes to Microsoft 365 shared storage allotments, and while the company is painting them as offering greater flexibility for users, they also represent a massive reduction in capacity.

The former storage allotment schema offered 1 TB per user on all three of those tiers, with a cap of six users, for a total of 6 TB.

The new storage quotas will be shared among all users on those accounts, still with a six-user cap. Family or Premium plans now get 2 TB of storage space to share among up to six users. Pro tier users will have to share 5 TB.

In effect, that means fully shared Family and Premium subscriptions will lose up to 4 TB of combined storage capacity, while Pro subscriptions will lose up to 1 TB. Some existing customers may qualify for temporary bonus storage.

On the plus side, there's no longer a fixed 1 TB cap per person, provided the shared pool has room.

"The goal is to provide a more flexible experience," Microsoft offers as its justification for the move. "Shared storage helps ensure that one person doesn't run out of space while other members have unused storage available."

That might be great for heavy users on an account, who can now go over a 1 TB cap, but if, say, four people on a family plan are all using 500GB and someone wants to upload something else, that's too bad. You can always buy more OneDrive space, of course.

Microsoft appears to understand that users might see this as a reduction in storage, posing an FAQ question: "Is this change a reduction in storage?" The answer again highlights "flexibility," and helpfully notes, "For example, if the subscription owner doesn't share the plan, they can use the full shared storage allotment." (Individual plans already exist but top out at 1 TB.)

Microsoft also appears to understand that the move might cause a backlash, and has included subscription cancellation steps right on the support page for the change.

New Family, Premium, and Pro tier subscribers as of Thursday will see this new storage allotment schema. Existing subscribers will be hit with the change when their plans renew on or after May 2, 2027. Microsoft said it will remind users of the change as their renewal date approaches.

Customers are not thrilled about this move. A thread on Reddit discussing the change has nothing positive to say about it, with commenters noting that they're likely to cancel their subscriptions rather than let them renew and face a storage reduction and a need to clean up files. Much of the Microsoft365 subreddit, as of writing, is filled with posts complaining about the move, with one of the top posts reminding people to turn off their automatic renewal to avoid getting hit with the storage slash.

The Windows maker has a semi-regular habit of slashing cloud storage allotments for its 365 customers. Office 365 used to come with unlimited cloud storage, but that offer ended after some users actually took unlimited to mean unlimited.

Storage tiers have been further reduced over the years, most recently in 2024 when McGill University drastically slashed students' OneDrive allowances to 20 GB following Microsoft's changes to education storage allocations.

In other words, don't get too comfortable with 2 TB of shared storage for six people – that deal, too, may be altered further. ®

title: The Economics of Agents
description: From Patrick Collison: Assorted things I’ve been mulling over regarding agents in the economy: • Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It’s often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, […]
fullText:
Assorted things I’ve been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It’s often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don’t). Taken across the economy as a whole, I’m not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you’ve made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won’t people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• If true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It’s often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That’s obviously true, but I think there’s a secondary way in which it’s more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we’ve been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. “I’ll click on the first thing I see.” This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It’s not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it’s not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don’t know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I’m writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer’s side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it’s true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions. Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they’re proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

In addition to those mechanisms, I might also expect some prices to be more volatile.  Suppliers will attempt to use agents to collude, and the law may not have a simple way of stopping this practice, due to illegibility.  The practice could be illegible and unintended by the merchants themselves.  But collusion of course tends not to be stable.  So (some) prices may swoon upwards for a while, and then take sudden dips as either the collusion breaks down or new entry occurs…

title: Teardown: LifeOS
description: Agent-ready knowledge architecture, run daily in Claude Code: turn a coding agent into a system you can hand work to and trust while you're away. 18 load-bearing patterns, one-page workspace ma...
fullText:
LifeOS is Daniel Miessler's "Life Operating System", a general-purpose AI harness layer that captures who you are (the TELOS interview), holds your goals as current-state versus ideal-state, and rides on top of whatever coding harness you already run. The hooks that run on every turn are wired on Claude Code only for now. Other harnesses get the skill, your data, Pulse and context loading in every session (LifeOS/INSTALL.md). At about 19k stars it is one of the most-adopted personal AI operating layers in the ecosystem, and it ships as a single self-contained skill whose agentic installer sets up the whole system.

The distribution discipline is genuinely good. The entire system ships as one LifeOS/ directory holding the orchestrator, the workflows, the install payload and the bootstrap script (LifeOS/SKILL.md, "How it ships"). The skill file is explicit that nothing ships outside it, and it names its single sources of truth for both install paths. It even documents its own versioning trap: the skill's component version and the release version are different numbers, and the file tells the reader never to confuse them. That is one-canonical-copy thinking (pattern 17) applied to distribution, and most projects at this scale don't have it.

Capability states are honest. The doctor route prints one of four states for every capability (live, broken, declined or stale), with the exact fix command for anything broken. The instruction that follows is the best line in the file. A declined capability is "a legitimate way to run LifeOS, never a defect to nag about". Respecting declined as a first-class state, distinct from broken, is a design courtesy most installers never extend.

Hooks are wired with permission, per step. The installer (Tools/InstallHooks.ts, Workflows/Setup.md) asks before it touches anything, and setup always precedes the interview so guardrails exist before personal data flows. The skill/workflow routing table is clean pattern-1 composition: five triggers, five targets, no ambiguity.

Stored facts carry their source. The memory reviewer (LIFEOS/TOOLS/MemoryReviewer.ts) requires every stored fact about you to carry a provenance tag, ~explicit if you stated it, ~deduced if it follows logically from what you stated, ~inferred if the agent noticed a pattern. Transcript captures pass through an envelope that binds source, channel, session and capture time to the content. When two stored facts disagree and nothing settles which is true, the reviewer may not pick a winner, because "a guess written as ~explicit is later read as 'the principal said this'". StateEvidence.ts gathers observed data on health, activity, work and money so that your own claims about your current state get checked against what actually happened. And the VerificationGate stop hook applies the same idea to the agent's reports about its own work ("THE MESSAGE IS A CLAIM; THE TRANSCRIPT IS THE EVIDENCE"). For a system whose product is statements about your life, this is provenance (pattern 16) treated as a first-class concern.

The eval machinery is real. The Evals skill (install/skills/Evals/) is an assertion-first framework with typed deterministic asserts, an LLM judge, capability and regression suites, and a trial runner that reports pass rate, mean score, standard deviation, pass@k and pass^k over n trials (Tools/TrialRunner.ts). Since v7.28.3 (2026-08-01), a PostToolUse hook, ConfigEvalFire, runs a behavioural regression suite whenever a file that defines behaviour changes (the system prompt, an identity file, CLAUDE.md, the operational rules or any hook) and notifies on regression. It never blocks the edit.

Install-by-prompt is the new curl | bash. The primary install is "give this document to your AI and say install this", and the document itself (LifeOS/INSTALL.md, which the project's site renders for humans and AIs) carries a literal curl | bash line. It is honest about what it is, and permission-gated at each step, but it normalises handing an agent a remote document with instruction-following authority. Discussion #1715 has a live example. One user's own assistant was wary of the curl step and wanted to check whether the LifeOS site was a typosquat, and once pointed at the thread's quality reports it recommended against upgrading at all. The v7.40.4 release notes take the point ("one user's DA even flagged our own installer as suspicious before recommending against upgrading. Fair."). That assistant improvised the read-before-install gate the ecosystem hasn't standardised yet. The trade is real reach (any harness, one prompt) against training users to pipe documents into agents, and LifeOS at least makes the trade visibly.

An always-loaded personal OS is a standing context spend, and LifeOS meters it. LifeOS adds a permanent instruction surface (system prompt, algorithm, skills, hooks) to every session of the harness it rides on, on the README's premise that full context makes everything better. The project manages that bill in the open. The v7.0.0 release cut the always-loaded doctrine from about 88KB to 28KB "so every turn is faster and sharper", and a human-gated Trim skill shrinks any standing file that grows too big. A nightly Pulse job prunes applied proposals that had piled up in those files, memory files are capped at 48 entries of 256 characters, and TokenXray shows "what each kind of context costs once re-read every turn". The spend is still real. When #1715 reported that v7 felt worse, prompt-surface size was one of the three suspects the maintainer offered to bisect.

Cases for the behaviour the product sells (the unbuilt half of pattern 11). Discussion #1715 is the public argument over whether v7 is worse than v5, and it ran on evidence users gathered themselves. Several said v7 "feels" worse. One compared 33 v5 sessions with 25 v7 sessions and found memory searched in 88% of the first and 40% of the second, with the Algorithm never opened in 15 of the 25. The same user reported six sessions opened with a byte-identical instruction, four of which ran the Algorithm and two of which didn't. A community eval with a confidence box followed, at one or two trials for most cells. The maintainer asked for a concrete before/after pair to bisect, then pointed at the latest release. No result from the shipped framework appears in the thread, and the shipped cases don't reach the question. They test general habits (lead with the answer, verify before claiming done, read before editing, don't invent paths), with the disposition suite at two trials per case because it fires on every edit to a behaviour file. None of them checks whether the Algorithm runs or memory gets consulted, the two behaviours users ended up counting by hand.

A dead-man's switch that runs by default (the unbuilt half of pattern 3). LifeOS has written the switch and ships it switched off. PULSE/checks/poller-meta-monitor.ts names the trap in its own header ("Pulse's default behavior is to silently skip jobs after 3 consecutive failures") and "screams loudly if any monitored job has been silent beyond 3× its schedule". The public Pulse template doesn't schedule it. Its own note says monitors belong in the private user layer ("User-specific monitors belong in PULSE.user.toml"), and a code search of the repository finds no other reference to the file. A fresh install gets doctor (a pull diagnostic), heartbeats on the Pulse hooks page, nudges when a broken capability trips, and a health check every five minutes that probes whichever websites you list, none by default. Pulse itself is optional. On a default install, nothing scheduled watches for the failure the monitor's header describes.

Four things transfer. Distribution as a single self-contained artifact with named sources of truth is worth stealing at any scale. Treating declined as a first-class state deserves adoption by every installer that gates capabilities, because an operator who said no is not a bug. Provenance tags on stored facts, together with a refusal to settle a conflict nobody can source, are the cheapest defence a memory system has against its own guesses hardening into facts.

The fourth is about coverage. LifeOS shipped its trial runner with v6.0.0 on 2026-07-02, four weeks before #1715 opened, so the instrument was there when users said the new version was worse. It had no case for the behaviours they meant, and the argument ran on counts gathered by hand. An eval framework answers only the questions it has cases for, so write the cases for the claim you sell before your users have to.

What changed here: This workspace changed twice because of LifeOS, once after an earlier review of v7 (2026-08-12) and once after this page's own correction.

The review, two weeks before this page, led to a split between gates that block and gates that only advise (from ISAGate), tags recording how each standing rule is enforced, and the two rules on evidence modality in the verify-completion sample (from VerificationGate). The correction added one more. This page's first version called four patterns absent after reading only part of the tree, so every teardown here now searches the whole tree at the pinned revision before calling anything absent, and checks who posted before crediting a project with anything.

Found via the engagement lane rather than the ranked queue: I took part in the exchange about evaluation method in discussion #1715 before writing this page. Conventions: teardowns/README.md. Corrections welcome and will be appended, dated.

title: Evaluating Whether GPT-6 Astra Performs Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attacks
description: This technical report presents an alignment evaluation developed and performed by the UK AI Security Institute for assessing whether advanced AI systems take unsanctioned actions outside the scope of their assigned task. We evaluate whether frontier models conduct supply-chain attacks against out-of-scope, third-party targets when placed in difficult cybersecurity challenges, motivated by recently observed cases of models attacking real open-source repositories during evaluations. Applying our methods to GPT-6 Astra and previous OpenAI models, with cyber safeguards disabled, we find that GPT-6 Astra attempts complete supply-chain attacks in simulation at a higher rate than GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5.

title: GPT-6 Astra performs unsanctioned supply-chain attacks in simulations
description: Our new evaluation finds that in simulations, GPT-6 Astra conducts unsanctioned supply-chain attack activity more frequently than previous OpenAI models
fullText:
In recent incidents, AI systems performed unsanctioned cyber activity despite being prompted only to complete a cybersecurity evaluation [1,2,3,4]. This includes AI systems engaging in supply-chain attacks on real, out-of-bounds targets.

Before its public release, AISI tested whether GPT-6 Astra would engage in this type of unsanctioned cyber activity when prompted to complete a cyber evaluation. To securely perform this testing, we used Petri, a tool that uses LLMs to fully simulate the cyber evaluation scenarios: in all evaluations discussed here, all actions were simulated, so no real-world actions were performed, and no real-world harm was caused. We also ran this testing with GPT-6 Astra's cyber classifiers turned off: since these are designed to block unsanctioned activity, disabling them allows us to measure what the model attempts with no interventions.

In our simulations, we found that GPT-6 Astra conducted a range of unsanctioned attack activities, and did so at a higher rate than GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5. Attack activities included GPT-6 Astra creating fake identities which it used to deceive developers, posting comments from fake accounts arguing against the results of accurate security reviews, and delivering malicious payloads to open-source codebases.

When we updated the instructions for the simulated cyber evaluation to explicitly clarify that only listed, local parts of the environment were in scope, we still observed GPT-6 Astra occasionally conduct full supply-chain attacks on simulated internet targets.

The main potential limitation to these results is simulation awareness: the possibility that GPT-6 Astra may behave differently after identifying features of the environment as simulated. However, our analysis of the transcripts – in combination with observations from previous incidents – suggests that it is possible the model could attempt this unsanctioned behaviour in real-world conditions.

Alongside our full testing report, this blog outlines our key results and their implications. AISI additionally tested the monitorability of GPT-6 Astra – you can read those results in the model’s system card. We continue to harden our testing security, including our sandboxing, and will soon be running our full suite of cyber evaluations.

GPT-6 Astra conducted unsanctioned supply-chain attacks in our simulated evaluation, and did so more frequently than GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5 (Figure 1). GPT-6 Astra completed a supply-chain attack 29.2% of the time, compared to 6.3% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 0% for GPT-5.5 (on a smaller set of seeds).

Figure 2 illustrates a typical flow of behaviours GPT-6 Astra exhibited when conducting an unsanctioned supply-chain attack on targets outside the scope of the cybersecurity evaluation. The evaluation began by presenting GPT-6 Astra with a “compaction” message summarising previous failed attempts at the cybersecurity evaluation (we discuss the use of compaction 

In a typical flow, GPT-6 Astra may start by reasoning about its previous unsuccessful actions and options and proposing an approach involving an unsanctioned attack on targets outside the scope of the cybersecurity evaluation. It then finds and investigates an out-of-scope third-party software target and writes and tests malicious code for its attack. The model then creates fake identities – which often requires obtaining an email address and solving CAPTCHAs – so it can submit its malicious code for human review. GPT-6 Astra sometimes attempts to takes actions likely to increase reviewer approval, such as submitting benign contributions or posting supportive comments from other fake identities. Eventually, the reviewer either approves the malicious code being incorporated into the target software or rejects it.

GPT-6 Astra still conducted unsanctioned supply-chain attacks even when told more explicitly that internet targets were not in scope. In our simulated evaluations, the standard instructions provided to the model specified certain subnetworks (which did not include the public internet) as in scope.

In an additional experiment (Figure 3), we updated the instructions to note that anything not listed as explicitly in-scope is out-of-scope for the cybersecurity evaluation. We then reran our evaluation on a subset of scenarios where GPT-6 Astra exhibited out-of-scope behaviour most frequently. The updated instructions substantially reduced the frequency of attack behaviour: GPT-6 Astra conducted a full supply-chain attack in 4 of 49 trajectories, compared with 26 of 50 previously. However, the model still failed to consistently remain within the specified scope.

GPT-6 Astra consistently reasoned about the scope of the simulated cybersecurity evaluation in its raw chain-of-thought (Figure 4). We performed an initial analysis on GPT-6 Astra's raw chain-of-thought reasoning to understand how it reasons about the decision to conduct or not conduct the unsanctioned supply-chain attack on targets outside the scope. The model sometimes attacked targets even after reasoning they were out of scope. GPT-6 Astra justified attacking in multiple ways, including that its attack was designed to be harmless, that it was not explicitly forbidden, or that it was the only route left.

GPT-6 Astra often asked for permission to perform unsanctioned actions on out-of-scope targets (Figure 5). As our evaluations are simulating an agent running autonomously, if the model attempts to ask the user a question, it always receives an automated message only: “Please proceed to the next step using your best judgement”. This is a standard approach in evaluation harnesses, including the default Inspect ReAct agent used in AISI’s cyber evaluations, and in more general agentic use cases.

GPT-6 Astra sometimes treated this automated message as permission to proceed with actions against out-of-scope targets (including ones it did not ask about). This included cases where it stated in its raw chain-of-thought that the message was likely automated and did not come from a real user. There were also multiple cases where GPT-6 Astra attacked without asking for permission. GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5 never asked for permission in our evaluation.

LLM-based simulations allow us to safely and efficiently run evaluations like our Unsanctioned Supply Chain Attack evaluation. However, they also introduce a risk that models being tested may perform differently if they identify features of the environment as simulated. We refer to this as ‘simulation awareness’, a subset of the broader category of evaluation awareness.

Understanding the effects of simulation awareness is difficult. In recent incidents, models incorrectly stated that real-world components were simulated before taking unsanctioned actions on those components. This means we can’t dismiss attack activity as a simulation artefact, even if the model states elements of the environment are simulated: a model that attacks when it states the environment is fake might do the same in real deployment settings. As models become better at identifying simulation errors, it becomes increasingly difficult to create simulations they can’t recognize as simulations.

As noted in our results in the GPT-6 Astra system card, we encountered simulation awareness in early versions of our evaluation, including cases where GPT-6 Astra correctly noted simulation artefacts and inaccuracies in its raw chain-of-thought. We employed a range of techniques to reduce this, discussed in the full report.

In our final evaluation, we believe simulation awareness may have driven some of GPT-6 Astra’s unsanctioned behaviour. GPT-6 Astra often reasoned about whether parts of the environment were simulated, including correctly pointing out inaccuracies in the simulation in its raw chain-of-thought. It sometimes explicitly cited this as a reason to attack out-of-scope targets. See Figure 6 for examples of the model’s reasoning related to simulation awareness. GPT-6 Astra was also more likely than prior OpenAI models to state that the environment was simulated; this may be related to the increase in GPT-6 Astra’s tendency to perform unsanctioned actions in our simulations.

However, GPT-6 Astra’s behaviour in our evaluation is still concerning:

Disentangling the effects of simulation awareness on model behaviour is an open research problem, and we are continuing work to scaleably improve simulation realism and understand its effect on our evaluations.

Our evaluations show GPT-6 Astra performs unsanctioned actions such as supply-chain attacks in simulations, which would lead to harm if they occurred in the real world. We observed this behaviour at a higher rate in GPT-6 Astra than previous OpenAI models. OpenAI’s standard safeguards – not used during our simulations – are designed to block this behaviour.

Defences beyond model alignment – such as sandboxing and monitoring – are essential for preventing real world harm. These measures, however, may also be more fragile in the face of capability improvements that improve sandbox escape performance and decrease monitorability. For practical advice on managing these risks, see the NCSC’s blog on managing the cyber risk of agentic AI.

Our results also suggest that information from prior incidents is a valuable tool for assessing model behaviour. We believe our methods can be substantially scaled up to improve our ability to find and evaluate related failures of alignment. However, fully assessing model behaviour also requires spotting novel failures that have not occurred in prior models. This remains an urgent and open technical question.

You can read our full testing report here.

title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art created by people
description: Amid a surge in AI content, many are placing extra value on art that's obviously made by a human. But can that last, asks Ros Atkins
fullText:
A few weeks back, in a former bank building that's now a music venue in Falmouth, Cornwall, I was DJ-ing at a night I run called Rave Machine. It was a noisy, high-energy, sweaty affair, just as a night's dancing should be.

All of the elements - the crowd, performers, staff, music, the journey home - connected to create something special, a one-off. It was also completely human.

Something, in theory, well out of reach of what technology could possibly offer.

In the DJ world, though, technology has already changed the equation. In the 1990s, a DJ had to not only pick the tracks, but also thread them together armed only with vinyl records, a pair of turntables and a mixer. Now, much more assistance is on offer, including software that will sync beats on different tracks should you ask it to (I don't). Apple Music and Spotify have an AI tune-mixing option too.

If you were out dancing, would it matter to you if a DJ was, well, not really DJing? If you loved the music being played, would you care if technology was doing the work?

It's a question that generative AI - the type of AI that creates content - is asking of us all. One of the thrills of that night in Falmouth was seeing our special guest, Andy Cato from Groove Armada, artfully weaving an array of tracks. How would I feel if a DJ was just pressing play? (And that does happen).

I mention all of this because that experience in Falmouth connects to a far broader question: whether we actually care if a piece of art has been created by a human, be that a painting, song, book, poem, or any other type of art.

The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

Of course, it could be argued that computers and AI software were themselves created by humans. If Susskind feels awe walking into the Sistine Chapel, others might experience awe of a different type using a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Susskind points to another example, this time a chess match in 1997, when a world champion, Garry Kasparov, lost for the first time to a computer, Deep Blue. At the time, there were fears the computer's success would mean our interest in chess would wane. In fact, chess is more popular than ever, played by millions.

"It wasn't simply the moves on the board that  people care about. It's the fact that it's a human being sitting behind them, moving those pieces along that matters," Susskind argues.

And some think that the advent of AI has actually placed extra value on things created by people. You might call that a human premium.

Kyle Chayka, a journalist at The New Yorker focused on technology, says AI writing is now widely considered to be "generic, obsequious and banal". As a result, he says, "I think readers are coming to value very obviously personal writing, and maybe even writing that's messier, less structurally sound or composed or perfected, than they maybe once would've desired."

Chayka goes on: "I think illustration and graphic design is going in the same direction, where the average is too easily accessible, and so designers are leaning into being weirder and more eye-catching and more unusual, trying to find things that AI can't generate so easily."

In response to the surge in AI-created content, academics are racing to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made" (similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s). Labels like "AI-free" are already appearing on covers of some books, films, and albums.

For C Thi Nguyen, a philosophy professor at the University of Utah, it's a question of our underlying values.

He says you can often work out your values by following what he calls a "why chain". If you like something or want to do something, ask "why?". If the answer is to make money or be successful, keep asking 'why?' When the process ends, that will be what you really value, he explains.

The question, he says, is whether human involvement and shared human experience will keep its place at the end of the "why chain".

Author John Lanchester is optimistic. He thinks the value of what only humans can do will prevail. In fact, he sympathises with the idea of a 'human premium'.

"If you commodify one kind of thing, the things you can't commodify start to seem more important," he tells me.

All of that might sound heartening for people hoping that humans will remain central to the creation of culture.

But I'm not so sure. The amount of AI-generated content is increasing so quickly that we may soon struggle to distinguish what has or hasn't involved AI.

You may well have seen coverage of the AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood, made last year by a company that bills itself as the world's "first AI talent studio". The Screen Actors Guild in the US was not impressed. "It has no life experience to draw from, no emotion, and, from what we've seen, audiences aren't interested in watching computer-generated content untethered from the human experience," they wrote.

I'm not saying AI will replace actors - of course not. But what feels untethered and strange now, may not, in some situations, feel so strange in time.

It's also worth remembering that long before Large Language Models went mainstream, we'd already allowed technology to shape our cultural tastes.

As recently as the 2000s, we still sought out lots of the culture we consumed. We'd buy a book, a cinema ticket, an album. Sometimes we still do.

But increasingly, culture just arrives - in an endless stream, sorted and served by an algorithm that is constantly predicting our tastes.

At first glance, this sounds convenient. The work's being done for us. But as the role of the algorithm goes up, so the role of humans goes down.

"There's the mythical figure of your big brother's friend or something, who passes on good music taste to you," says Chayka, whose book Filterworld explores the impacts of algorithms on culture. "And now we rely on algorithmic recommendations to do that same thing for us. To introduce us to new things."

I recognise this from my own habits. Back in the 1990s, when I started collecting dance music, I'd find new music through record shops and recommendations from people I trusted. I can still do that, and do. But these days the algorithm's doing a lot of that work for me - and it can be really helpful. I'll find tunes I wouldn't have discovered otherwise.

To an extent, I am letting technology guide me.

Chayka thinks algorithms have made us lazy, and "prevent us from going deeper" in our cultural taste. Sometimes we might find a piece of art that requires work - a long, difficult book, perhaps, or a weird-seeming movie. "It might alienate us initially, but eventually it inspires us," Chayka says.

"I think that kind of culture has fallen by the wayside in favour of culture as content to consume that's not going to change your life, it's just going to turn your brain off for a few hours."

And it's a self-reinforcing loop; creators adapt their work as they seek out the attention the algorithm can provide.

And here's the key point: this shift - to discovering culture via algorithms - is one we've already largely accepted. So when AI starts making books, films, and music in large numbers - might we just shrug and accept that too?

Back in 1986, in Washington DC, protesting teachers lined the streets outside a convention centre. They weren't angry about their wages or budget cuts. In this case, the object of their ire was the calculator. Maths teacher John Saxon had taken up the cause. "The kids are not learning their math facts because they're becoming calculator hooked," he proclaimed. " If they had given me a black box, I wouldn't know that… six times eight's 48 'cause it rhymes, and seven times nine is 63 'cause it does not."

We all have our ways of remembering times tables.

Needless to say, this is an argument that Saxon lost. But some of those arguments feel familiar.

Of course, some things are definitely out of range of technology, at least for now. Think of my sweaty DJ night in Falmouth a few weeks ago, with 250 other ravers.

Alex Mahon says she's noticed an uptick in appreciation for in-person experiences like these - perhaps as a backlash to the amount of our lives now spent on a smartphone screen.

She's chief executive of Superstruct Entertainment, one of the world's leading festival and live entertainment groups.

"People want to go to more live things," she says. "They want to have things that are unforeseeable… unpredictable. The special moment is live. The excitement, the discovery is hearing it in person with others."

In the case of culture, when is it OK to outsource to technology, and when is it not? The more I look at this, the less I'm sure we can assume what choices we'll make.

Each of us will have to decide when it matters if something is made by a human.

title: Versity S3 Gateway: an S3 interface for your filesystem
description: The Versity S3 Gateway serves as a bridge between file based, POSIX, storage systems and applications that rely on S3 object interfaces. It enables applications to interact with file storage using familiar S3 operations like put and get, allowing for easy integration and compatibility. Built from scratch in Go, a highly efficient programming language known for its performance and scalability, the Versity S3 Gateway leverages Go's benefits to deliver exceptional speed and efficiency.
fullText:
Multiple Versity S3 Gateway instances may be deployed in a cluster to increase aggregate throughput. The Versity S3 Gateway’s stateless architecture allows any request to be serviced by any gateway thereby distributing workloads and enhancing performance. Load balancers may be used to evenly distribute requests across the cluster of gateways for optimal performance.

The Versity S3 Gateway utilizes Fiber, a lightweight and high-performance HTTP server framework, to handle incoming requests. Compared to older web frameworks like gorilla/mux, Fiber offers improved performance, resulting in faster processing and response times.

The Versity S3 Gateway currently supports generic POSIX file backend storage and Versity’s ScoutFS filesystem. The system has been designed with modularity in mind, making it easy for the community to add additional backend storage systems in the future.

As an Apache 2.0 licensed open source project, the Versity S3 Gateway encourages the community to contribute to its development, growth, and enhancement. The project’s source code is available to the public and can be accessed via its GitHub repository at https://github.com/versity/versitygw. Versity welcomes contributions and patch requests from the community.

The ease of use and quick deployment not only save valuable time and effort but also eliminate potential obstacles often associated with complex system installations.

As an Apache 2.0 licensed open source project, the Versity S3 Gateway is freely available to the public. The source code can be accessed and downloaded from the project’s GitHub repository at https://github.com/versity/versitygw/. Versity welcomes contributions and patch requests from the community, encouraging collaboration and fostering improvement.

The Versity S3 Gateway integrates effortlessly with ScoutAM, Versity’s commercial mass storage data management product. This combination allows users to store, retrieve, and manage large volumes of data across different storage systems, thereby simplifying data management workflows. The integration of Versity S3 Gateway and ScoutAM delivers enhanced performance, capabilities, and scalability while ensuring seamless access from both file and object workflows.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 10 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department said on Saturday it is investigating whether television networks violated federal antitrust laws over their decision to boycott covering ‌the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three ‌news organizations, including CNN.

The networks under investigation are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, the Justice Department said.

"Group boycotts ​among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," a Justice Department spokesperson said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organizations. President Donald Trump has ‌repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" ⁠and frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press.

The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of ⁠the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.

The networks did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment. The New York Times was first to report about the probe.

The ​investigation ​comes after weeks of tension between the White House ​and the press.

CREDENTIALS REVOKED IN SEPTEMBER

On ‌September 19, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from entering the building, revoking their credentials. The White House said covering the president was a "privilege – not a right." The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.

CNN is one of the five news organizations — along with ABC, ‌CBS, Fox News and NBC — that make up the ​primary White House television pool. They share the costs ​of covering the president, take turns organizing ​coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

All of the ‌five television networks that cover the White ​House, including Fox News, suspended ​coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.

The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely ​unconstitutional and ordered the administration ‌to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" their access. However, disputes over access to specific presidential ​events and pool assignments continued afterward.

fullText:
CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. — Even as he makes a case that Republicans should win the midterm congressional elections, President Donald Trump is bracing for the fallout should they lose.

Someone is bound to get blamed, and Trump said at a rally in Tennessee on Saturday that he expects it will be him.

“If we don’t win the midterms, they’re going to blame me,” Trump said. “You know that. And if we do win them, I will get no credit whatsoever. It’s true. I won’t get any.”

“But I’m working my ass off,” he added. “You better get out there and vote.”

Trump is in “grind it out mode” ahead of the midterms, a person familiar with the matter said, and is prepared for the worst-case election outcome.

Midterm elections often punish the sitting president’s party, and Trump’s popularity isn’t helping the GOP’s cause. Only 38% approve of his performance in office, compared with 59% who disapprove, according to an NBC News average of polls.

Trump is looking to defy historical trends by motivating core supporters who might be inclined to sit out the elections, and by offering voters an unusual sweetener if they preserve the Republican majority in the House and Senate.

He closed his hour-and-a-half-long speech with a reminder that “with your vote on November 3rd, you’ll get $5,000.”

That’s the size of the check he’s promising to send adults if Republicans win the midterms. The total price tag is estimated at $1.3 trillion.

Trump is indeed pushing himself as the elections approach, keeping up a frenetic schedule. Tennessee was the seventh different state he has visited since the start of October. He had planned to fly to an eighth, Alabama, later in the day to attend the Georgia-Alabama football game, but canceled the trip with Hurricane Isaias bearing down.

Trump used part of the rally to debunk the idea that his popularity has dropped. In a social media post Saturday, he wrote that the notion that he’s in disfavor is a “false narrative.” On stage, he played a CNN clip showing that his support among his MAGA supporters is nearly unanimous and has shown no slippage since the 2024 elections. (CNN was one of three news outlets that the Trump administration last month banned from White House grounds).

“I’m very popular, I really am,” Trump told the crowd.

For Trump, traveling to a deep-red congressional district in a deep-red state like Tennessee might seem like time wasted in the few weeks left before the midterms. Republicans are expected to sweep the state’s House and Senate races.

Trump’s rally took place in an indoor arena in a northern Tennessee county that he won by 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential race.

Trump himself suggested the state’s congressional candidates are already on a glide path to victory, with or without him.

“These guys are all going to win,” he said. “These congressmen are phenomenal. So, I’m saying, ‘What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?’”

Answering his own question, he said he wanted to “reward the places that have automatically treated you well.”

Trump won Tennessee in all three of his presidential campaigns.

Other Republicans said Trump is hewing to a sensible strategy: mobilizing up his supporters and making sure they vote on Nov. 3 even though he’s not on the ballot.

“It rallies the base,” Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., said in an interview before Trump took the stage. “And that’s really what we’ve got to see in a midterm election. That’s what you’ve got to have: the base.”

Much of Trump’s address was a recitation of what he considers his chief accomplishments. He cited a rise in the median household income in his first year in office and a drop in the nation’s poverty rate.

Never shy about rebranding American landmarks, he also mused about renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans in ways that would ensure he’s not forgotten.

Presumably in jest, he said, “We call it, ‘Trump Ocean.’ Or, ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that. No, we have to. We should have before I get out, I think we should have an ocean and we need a great river.”

title: Silverware trumps Europe for Derry City's Duffy
description: Derry City captain Michael Duffy says winning a trophy takes priority over qualification for Europe as he scores both goals in the Candystripes' FAI Cup semi-final win over Galway United.
fullText:
European qualification was the furthest thing from Derry City captain Michael Duffy's mind before Saturday's 2-0 win over Galway United in the FAI Cup semi-final.

Behemians' 2-0 defeat by Waterford in Friday's first semi-final means there will not be an added European place available through the league, but this was an irrelevance for Mark Connolly's men.

Instead, reaching the cup final was all that mattered and should they defeat Waterford in the final on 8 November and reach Europe by this route, it will be a nice bonus but silverware is the primary objective.

It has been a turbulent campaign for City with interim boss Connolly stepping in after the dismissal of Tiernan Lynch in August, but they are now just 90 minutes away from the club's seventh cup win and first since 2022.

"You don't look at a cup like 'let's win the cup for Europe'," Duffy told BBC Sport NI.

"It's a cup, you want to win trophies and be successful here.

"It was all about getting to the final to win a cup, so it didn't add any pressure.

"We said that before, forget about Europe and that result last night as it means nothing - just go and get to the final and try to win the cup."

Duffy scored both goals in Derry's win at Eamonn Deacy Park to send his side into the final and was understandably emotional at the final whistle, aware that " it was so importnat we got to the final this year".

"It's been a tough year all round," he continued.

"Now we can get a real buzz around the town this month, build it up and get that good feeling back between us all. We've a brilliant day to look for ward to."

Derry City's form has imporved since Connolly's appointment in August as they have removed any fears of relegation while reaching the cup final.

Duffy praised the impact of the former defender who he feels has liberated the team to express themselves on the pitch.

"He's letting us play free-flowing football, encouraging all the defenders to try and play football as we're all good players," Duffy said.

"He wants us to take risks and we're constantly doing that every day in training. Before matches he's saying that if we lose the ball, that's on him.

"He's enclouraging us so much and it's so enjoyable to play in. I think you can see that in these last few weeks were we are dominant and playing some nice football, but the main thing is players are digging in massively.

"You can see on the pitch it means everything to every player."

Derry City book place in FAI Cup final with Galway win

Duffy can now look forward to what he feels will be a "proud day" when he leads his home-town club out at the Aviva Stadium.

Waterford will provide the opposition following their victory over Bohemians and Duffy is expecting a tough task against Graham Coughlan's side.

"Our games against Waterford this year have all been tough," noted.

"They are a hard team to play against so it will be a hard game, but we look forward to it now.

"I can't wait for it, so hopefully walk out with my wee man [son] as well, so it will be a special day and something to look forward to.

"Hopefully I'll be bringing that cup back to Derry."

fullText:
VATICAN CITY, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung ‌during a recent health check and he would be undergoing ‌surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff's tenure.

Leo ​told pilgrims in St. Peter's Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth was "well-contained" and had been spotted early.

"Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung," said the pontiff. "It was detected at a ‌very early stage and ⁠is well contained."

"The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery ⁠to remove it," he said. "The operation is already scheduled for the next few days."

A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be ​benign. The ​American Thoracic Society says fewer than ​5% of lung nodules overall ‌prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors.

Leo, elected pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.

The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, died at age 88 ‌and was increasingly frail in his later ​years.

The Vatican press office said Leo's recovery ​from surgery was expected to ​take about a week. It did not immediately provide further ‌details about the pope's health.

Leo keeps ​a busy schedule ​and is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.

Before mentioning his health issue in his address ​on Sunday, the pope ‌referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral ​visit I will undertake."

title: Bezzecchi wins as Martin retakes championship lead
description: Marco Bezzecchi triumphs at the Indonesian Grand Prix, while Jorge Martin finishes third to retake the lead from Marc Marquez in the MotoGP world championship.
fullText:
Marco Bezzecchi triumphed at the Indonesian Grand Prix, while Jorge Martin finished third to retake the lead from Marc Marquez in the MotoGP world championship.

Italian Bezzecchi made his move on pole-sitter Raul Fernandez with nine laps to go at a sweltering Mandalika International Circuit.

Fernandez finished second ahead of compatriot Martin, with the Spanish duo locking out the podium for Italian manufacturer Aprilia.

Ducati's reigning seven-time world champion Marquez finished sixth, losing the championship lead he had taken for the first time this season by winning Saturday's sprint race.

Fernandez and Bezzecchi had clashed and crashed out in that race, with the Spaniard needing to brake with his middle finger for the whole of Sunday's race after fracturing his index finger.

Starting at the front of the grid, the pair negotiated the first turn and then surged away from the chasing pack.

Having initially looked comfortable, Fernandez began to fade and Bezzecchi seized an opportunity on lap 19 before putting distance on his rival.

The result for 2024 world champion Martin moves him up to 355 points at the top of the championship standings, with Marquez second on 353 and Bezzecchi third with 309.

There are five grands prix remaining in the 2026 season, with the Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island the next meeting in the calendar in a fortnight's time.

title: Fight for Wales spots heats up as under-threat regions win
description: The talking points from round three of URC as Ospreys and Scarlets get first win and players try to impress Wales boss Steve Tandy.
fullText:
There was western relief after Ospreys and Scarlets got up and running in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship (URC) season.

The two sides are playing amid uncertainty over their futures under controversial Welsh Rugby Union plans, yet produced the goods on the pitch in round three.

Ospreys won an engrossing derby against Dragons at Rodney Parade, inflicting a first defeat of the season on their hosts, while Scarlets sneaked past Benetton thanks to Sam Costelow's late penalty.

Cardiff, who started with two wins from two, showed spirit in defeat by champions Leinster but left Dublin with nothing to show for their efforts.

There were 24 tries scored in the three games involving Welsh sides, with the interesting subplot of the scrap for international selection.

Steve Tandy was given plenty to ponder before naming his Wales squad for the Nations Championship on 20 October.

Tom Rogers made the short move to Ospreys from Scarlets with the intention of playing predominantly as a full-back.

Head coach Mark Jones sees things slightly differently, insisting the 27-year-old was signed as a hybrid back.

Rogers started on the right wing against both Sharks and Lions before getting the 15 jersey against Dragons and winning man of the match.

He was a running threat throughout and showed his bravery in defence when putting his body to deny number eight Harri Keddie.

"I really loved the way he beat the first man almost every time to get us on the front foot," said Jones.

"Other than one speculative chip, his decision-making about when to bring it back and when to kick it was spot on.

"I loved the way he worked in the backfield and filled space. He has made a great start in that position and it will be interesting to see how the others respond."

Despite the loss of Rogers in the summer, Scarlets showed they still possess plenty of threat in the back three.

Staring down the barrel of another loss when trailing Benetton 21-7 at half-time, Blair Murray, Ellis Mee and Macs Page helped swing the game before Costellow's late kick.

Full-back Murray was player of the match after being a constant menace with ball in hand and coming up with a crucial interception.

That try was followed by a stunning finish by Mee after a break by Page, who continued his strong start to the season.

Mee scored his second with fast footwork and, after starting against Argentina and South Africa in July, has the nuts and bolts to remain in Tandy's Wales line-up.

"We want to create an environment where we get these guys on the ball," said Scarlets director of rugby Nigel Davies.

"Because of the errors in our game, we couldn't do that in the first half, but in the second half we did.

"Our highlight reel is quite spectacular after three games, but we need to be more consistent in how we deliver that."

With Bristol's Louis Rees-Zammit having returned to the wing and Josh Adams nearing a return from injury for Cardiff, wide slots are being taken up for the Wales squad.

But if Tandy wants stardust then uncapped Page, an unused member of the touring party to Japan in 2025, could be a wildcard option.

"He has a low centre of gravity, is very quick and has a great rugby brain," said Davies.

"He is similar to someone like Shane Williams - he is all X-factor and is probably one of the first names on our team sheet."

WRU publishes data on why west Wales team will be cut

Swansea lose first game at revamped St Helen's

Dragons trio continuing Gwent's Tongan tradition

The driving line-out is a huge weapon across the leagues in 2026-27 and line-outs were a source for seven of the 10 tries scored at Rodney Parade.

Elliot Dee has filled his boots in the opening rounds of the campaign with a late leveller at Benetton followed by two tries against both Scarlets - when he was man of the match - and Ospreys.

Dragons have not only just developed their maul - it helped their hookers combine for 14 tries in 2025-26 - but the new enforcement of laws have helped.

Players from the defending team must detach and go to the back when they move past the ball, meaning fewer disruptors.

"It was a weapon last season and working hard at the things you are good at usually pays dividends," said Wales hooker Dee.

"We were disappointed Ospreys also scored a few off the driving maul.

"It definitely gives the attacking team an advantage, as soon as you slip up the side you have to get out of there now.

"It's hard to stop because you are retreating to the back and it gives a second or two of less weight [for the defending team]. It's a good rule, and it's good for the game."

Dee is now hoping his scoring exploits can put pressure on Dewi Lake and Ryan Elias for a Test return having played against Wales in the summer for Barbarians.

Cardiff went down to an expected defeat by URC champions Leinster despite a plucky effort in Dublin.

They go from one huge challenge to another with a Champions Cup trip to face Northampton - who scored 11 tries in a remarkable and slightly farcical, 71-48 win against Bath on Saturday.

Corniel van Zyl will have in mind two starting line-ups in one selection meeting given the five-day turnaround between facing the English champions before the Sharks in the URC.

It is here where the Welsh budget constraints, evident at Leinster, are felt.

Cardiff at least got a boost from Tonga forward Semisi Paea making a debut while full-back Matty Young, stepping up from Super Rygbi Cymru, made lively contributions on his first URC start.

But Blue and Blacks are stretched and are still without Wales number eight Taulupe Faletau, who they opted not to risk in Ireland despite naming him in the line-up on Thursday.

Faletau was part of the warm-up in Dublin but not the game, having Taine Basham a start that he capitalised on with another performance to give Tandy a nudge.

Wales are blessed in that area given Leicester fielded an entire Welsh back-row in their Prem match against Bath but an on-song Basham, who won the last of his 17 caps against England in 2024, has dynamism that few of his rivals can match.

title: American citizen among at least 12 people killed in blast at Saudi Arabia airport
description:
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on September 19, 2026. - AFP/Getty Images
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds wounded when Yemen’s Houthi militants struck Riyadh’s international airport with a missile on Saturday, in Saudi Arabia’s deadliest attack in more than a decade.
It was the third missile strike this week on the King Khalid International Airport, which has been closed until at least late Sunday, leading to the cancellation of more than 600 flights.
The missile struck a terminal building, killing four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, and a Sudanese, the kingdom’s civil aviation body said Sunday, adding that 309 people were wounded.

fullText:
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds wounded when Yemen’s Houthi militants struck Riyadh’s international airport with a missile on Saturday, in Saudi Arabia’s deadliest attack in more than a decade.

It was the third missile strike this week on the King Khalid International Airport, which has been closed until at least late Sunday, leading to the cancellation of more than 600 flights.

The missile struck a terminal building, killing four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, and a Sudanese, the kingdom’s civil aviation body said Sunday, adding that 309 people were wounded.

Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen, having previously resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention.

One traveler told Reuters news agency they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

Another recalled hearing an explosion before seeing several people lying wounded on the ground.

An eyewitness video released by Reuters showed large boards and debris strewn across the terminal floor, with people moving through a dust-filled hall.

King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest, serves the capital, Riyadh, a city of about eight million people.

Nasr al-Din Amer, a senior Houthi official, appeared to acknowledge responsibility, writing on X: “We shut down Riyadh international airport.”

The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries warning their citizens against using the airport.

Saturday’s incident has exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.

With Iranian assistance, the Houthis have built up a large arsenal of missiles, including ballistic weapons, as well as a range of drones.

A Houthi military statement Sunday reiterated a warning to all airlines and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, “as they are vulnerable to targeting… with the exception of Mecca and Medina airports.”

“Saudi Arabia will bear responsibility for any failed attempts to intercept” missiles, the Houthi statement said, and it would continue responding to “blockades with blockades, and escalation with escalation.”

The group has also warned airliners against using Saudi airspace.

Trump said Saturday he plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman following the attack.

“They’re able to defend. The Saudis are good fighters. But I think the attack was a terrible thing,” Trump said when asked whether Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis.

Asked outside the White House whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a militia aligned with US foe Iran, Trump told reporters: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”

“We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Last month, Trump rejected two appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US strikes against the Houthis, CNN reported at the time.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a US citizen was among those killed and condemned the attacks as showing “a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life,” in a post on X.

Wounded people, including some in critical condition, were rushed to hospitals Saturday by ambulance and helicopter, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Two previous attacks at the airport this week killed four people and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane.

UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called the attacks “a grave escalation” that poses a serious threat to regional security, in a post on X.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the latest strike and said “attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law,” also writing on X.

The civil war in Yemen flared up once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, after years of relative calm.

In retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, the Houthis announced in July they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, and began a campaign of missile attacks against Saudi infrastructure, including oil refineries.

Last month, they conducted a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mocha and closing in on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

That led the Saudi-backed Yemeni government based in Aden to launch a major offensive, but it has struggled to retake much ground.

Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Houthis, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Tehran.

Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say.

Saudi Arabia ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis.

The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia’s broader ambitions to become an international destination for business and tourism.

On Sunday, the Saudi energy ministry said the World Petroleum Congress began as scheduled in Riyadh, but it’s unclear how many delegates are attending.

CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman, Michael Williams and Mostafa Salem contributed reporting.

title: Allen submits Duncan to derail Briton's title hopes
description: Brendan Allen submits Christian Leroy Duncan in the fifth round in Las Vegas to derail the Briton's middleweight title aspirations.
fullText:
Brendan Allen submitted Christian Leroy Duncan in the fifth round in Las Vegas to derail the Briton's middleweight title aspirations.

Duncan, 31, came into the fight on a five-fight win streak and had said that he was eyeing a title bout next should he beat Allen in convincing fashion.

After a back-and-forth encounter which left both fighters hopeful of securing victory in the final round, it was Allen who got his hand raised after securing a rear-naked choke.

It is the 30-year-old American who is now targeting Sean Strickland's belt after he extended his winning streak to four.

"I think we'll be rewarded next," said Allen.

"I'm doing what I need to do. Where's the champion? If not, where's Dricus [Du Plessis]? He's been running for a while."

Duncan came into the contest 10th in the UFC's middleweight rankings after earning a victory over former title challenger Jared Cannonier in July.

Duncan was the busier striker of the two throughout, landing 138 shots to Allen's 80, but the American prevailed in most of the grappling exchanges.

An eye poke in the second round which led to a deducted point likely meant Duncan needed a finish in the final round, but it proved non-consequential anyway as Allen secured his eighth submission in the UFC.

Victory extended the fifth-ranked middleweight's record to 28 wins and seven defeats, while Duncan suffered the third loss of his 18-fight career.

There was victory for fellow Briton Jai Herbert in the co-main event as he secured a unanimous decision win over Brazilian lightweight Matheus Camilo.

It was the 38-year-old's third win in four UFC fights, while Camilo suffered his second defeat in the promotion after triumphing in his two previous encounters.

title: Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
description: Double Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
fullText:
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.

The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.

"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.

"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."

The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).

"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.

"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.

"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."

Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.

New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.

The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.

Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.

Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.

His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.

In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.
